PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                           )       Docket Nos. ER26-3380-000 and

                          REQUEST FOR REHEARING
         TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM EXCESSIVE TRANSMISSION RATES
                                    BY
                  OFFICE OF THE OHIO CONSUMERS’ COUNSEL



I.         INTRODUCTION

           The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”) September 29, 2026 Orders1 in

this case fail to protect consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”) from the risks and costs that will result from general acceptance of PJM’s Reliability

Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) proposal in these dockets. That order allows PJM to implement a

one-time capacity auction, with “billion-dollar implications for consumers,”2 to procure

generating capacity needed to serve forecasted load associated with large data centers and the

resulting resource adequacy shortfall in the 2028/2029 Delivery Year capacity auction.

           But the RBP auction design subjects consumers who are not causing the need for the

auction to shoulder the significant risk of paying for those costs, especially if the forecasted loads

do not materialize. FERC’s acceptance of this proposal is inconsistent with the stated

understandings of several of the commissioners in their concurring opinions. For example,

Commissioner David A. LaCerte states in his concurrence that the “Reliability Backstop


1
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 196 FERC ¶ 61,245 (2026) (“September 29 Order”).
2
    Id., Chairman Laura V. Swett concurring at P 2.

                                                          1
 Procurement is designed to make sure the costs of the large load at issue here are appropriately

allocated to that load and not to other consumers”3 Similarly, Commissioner Lindsay S. See

stated in her concurrence that:

           “customers that drive new costs should bear appropriate responsibility for
           them. Existing customers should not be left paying costs attributable to new
           demand. That principle is particularly important here where PJM proposes a
           backstop procurement specifically to deal with the capacity shortfall that
           rapid load growth largely drove.”4

The approved RBP auction design does not comport with these understandings. Moreover, the

FERC-accepted auction design does not contain sufficient and critically needed consumer

protections against the exercise of market power. Pursuant to Section 313 of the Federal Power

Act (“FPA”), 16 U.S.C. § 825l, and Rule 713 of the FERC’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18

C.F.R. § 385.713, the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”) hereby requests

rehearing of the September 29 Orders.

           OCC is the statutory representative of millions of Ohio residential utility consumers, per

R.C. Chapter 4911. OCC actively advocates for Ohioans in numerous state and federal

regulatory proceedings, including proceedings before FERC. OCC timely intervened in this case

on August 14, 2026,5 and submitted a Protest of the filing on August 21, 2026.6 Ohio residential

consumers are adversely affected by FERC’s September 29 Order in this case because they are at

risk of paying the costs for the capacity to be acquired by the auction even though they did not

cause that capacity to be procured. They are also at risk of paying an excessive capacity clearing

II.         BACKGROUND

            FERC generally accepted (subject to refund and paper hearing) PJM’s proposal to

establish the RBP, a one-time auction to procure 6,831 MW of new generating capacity and cure

the capacity shortage that occurred in the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) capacity base

residual auction for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.7 Although the September 29 Order generally

accepted the RBP proposal subject to refund and paper hearing, it postponed that auction for five

months, until February 28, 2027.8 This delay appears intended to give PJM time to modify the

proposal to correct certain deficiencies identified by FERC in the Order.9

            The overall RBP auction design accepted in the September 29 Order (subject to refund

and paper hearing) requires all loads in the transmission zones affected by the capacity shortages

from the 2028/2029 Delivery Year RPM auction to participate in the RBP auction.10 FERC’s

ruling accepts (a) the must-offer requirement for capacity sellers;11 (b) the $555/MW-day market

seller offer cap;12 (c) the pay-as-bid auction clearing mechanism proposal;13 (d) the shortage

penalty of 20% of the seller’s cleared bid times the shortage amount;14 (e) the lack of a locational

 requirement for new generation;15 and the opt-out provision for Fixed Resource Requirement

entities.16

            FERC found that the following elements of the RBP proposal may be unjust and

unreasonable, and set these issues for further paper hearings and additional comments: (a)

allocation of costs to Electric Distributor zones and then among Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”)

located in those zones using a snapshot-in-time approach that does not make adjustments for

changes in load over time;17 (b) the proposal to allow municipal and cooperative utilities to opt

out of allocated shares of the cost of capacity acquired through the RBP auction;18 (c) the

proposed rules for exit fees associated with a Transmission Owner leaving PJM that would

allocate the exit fees to Transmission Owners rather than LSEs;19 and (d) the LSE collateral

requirements.20 The September 29 Order also establishes a process for the paper hearing, but

states that FERC might be willing to delay that paper hearing process if PJM submits a filing

within 30 days of the date of the order to correct the deficiencies identified above.21

III.        SPECIFICATIONS OF ERRORS ON REHEARING

            1.       FERC erred by acting in an arbitrary and capricious manner in approving the

excessive $555/MW-day market seller offer cap and the pay-as-bid clearing mechanism design

for the RBP auctions. There is no evidence in the record to support this offer cap, and there is no

evidence to support the pay-as-bid clearing mechanism design. The excessive cap and pay-as-

                                                     4
 bid design will neither mitigate market power of sellers in the auction nor protect consumers in

Ohio and elsewhere in PJM from paying excessive, unjust and unreasonable capacity prices.

        2.      FERC erred in approving the pay-as-bid clearing mechanism design in the RBP

because this ruling departs from long-held precedent regarding the need for a single clearing

price auction structure in capacity auctions to mitigate seller market power.

        3.      FERC erred by acting in an arbitrary and capricious manner in approving the

proposed insufficient shortage penalty. That penalty is significantly less stringent than warranted

given the high risk associated with purchasing generating capacity through the RBP auction well

in advance of the forecasted new large data center loads materializing on the system. This ruling

is also inconsistent with FERC precedent establishing more stringent penalties for RPM capacity

resource non-performance, and inconsistent with judicial precedent requiring FERC to address

the critical issues raised before it.

        4.      FERC erred by acting in an arbitrary and capricious manner in approving an RBP

auction design that does not allocate the costs of the auction to the large load data centers

causing the need for the auction and thus placing residential consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in

PJM that did not cause these costs to be incurred at risk of paying these costs.

IV.     LIST OF ISSUES ON REHEARING

        1.      Whether FERC’s approval of the $555/MW-day seller offer cap for the RBP

auctions and the pay-as-bid clearing mechanism design are contrary to the Administrative

FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 136 S. Ct. 760, 782 (2016) (“EPSA”) (quoting Motor Vehicle

Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)); and Neighborhood TV

Co. v. FCC, 742 F.2d 629, 639 (D.C. Cir. 1984) (“Neighborhood TV Co.”) (the court must be

decision it reached”) because the excessive offer cap in conjunction with the pay-as-bid clearing

mechanism will not sufficiently constrain market power in the RBP auction?

       2.       Whether FERC’s approval of the pay-as-bid clearing mechanism in the RBP

proposal is arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act’s “arbitrary

and capricious” standard, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), Sithe/Indep. Power Partners, L.P. v. FERC, 165

Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)); and Neighborhood TV Co. v. FCC, 742 F.2d 629,

       3.       Whether FERC’s approval of the shortage penalty proposal is arbitrary and

capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act’s “arbitrary and capricious” standard,

5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), Sithe/Indep. Power Partners, L.P. v. FERC, 165 F.3d 944, 948 (D.C. Cir.

1999) (“Sithe/Indep. Power Partners”), FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 136 S. Ct. 760, 782

(2016) (“EPSA”) (quoting Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 463 U.S.

29, 43 (1983)); and Neighborhood TV Co. v. FCC, 742 F.2d 629, 639 (D.C. Cir. 1984)

considerations before the [agency] to the decision it reached.”) because the penalty is

disproportionate to the risk that residential consumers will bear if the large data center loads do

not materialize, is allocated to loads that did not cause the circumstances leading to the

imposition of the penalty, is inconsistent with judicial precedent requiring FERC to address the

critical issues raised before it, and is inconsistent with FERC precedent establishing more

stringent penalties for RPM capacity resource non-performance, contrary to the requirements of

Williams Gas Processing-Gulf Coast Co. v. FERC, 475 F.3d 319, 326 (D.C. Cir. 2006)

(“Williams Gas Processing”) (citing Brusco Tug & Barge Co. v. NLRB, 247 F.3d 273, 278 (D.C.

       4.      Whether FERC’s failure to allocate the RBP costs that will be incurred to serve

large data center loads to those loads is arbitrary and capricious in violation of the

Administrative Procedure Act’s “arbitrary and capricious” standard, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A),

Sithe/Indep. Power Partners, L.P. v. FERC, 165 F.3d 944, 948 (D.C. Cir. 1999) (“Sithe/Indep.

Power Partners”), FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 136 S. Ct. 760, 782 (2016) (“EPSA”)

(quoting Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)),

and Neighborhood TV Co. v. FCC, 742 F.2d 629, 639 (D.C. Cir. 1984) (“Neighborhood TV Co.”)

(the court must be able to “discern a reasoned path from the facts and considerations before the

[agency] to the decision it reached.”) because it violates long-held judicial principles that require

allocation of costs to those causing the costs to be incurred or benefiting from the projects?

 V.         REQUEST FOR REHEARING

A.         FERC’s approval of the $555/MW-day seller offer cap and the pay-as-bid clearing
           mechanism design for the RBP auction fails the test for reasoned decision-making
           because these decisions are not supported by the evidence and do not provide
           adequate protections for consumers against seller market power.

            FERC failed to provide a reasoned explanation for its acceptance of the $555/MW-day

proposed market seller offer cap and the pay-as-bid clearing mechanism for the RBP auction

design. This design will not protect consumers in Ohio or elsewhere in PJM from the exercise of

seller market power. In his Protest to the filing, the Independent Market Monitor for PJM

(“IMM”) demonstrates the critical flaw in PJM’s proposal, i.e., that PJM explicitly decided

not to use “market power screening or mitigation measures” in the design of the auction

parameters.22 As the IMM argues, “[i]t should be unacceptable that PJM, at a time of severe

supply shortage, would propose to not use the standard market power screening that is used

in all PJM capacity auctions.”23 This is especially concerning given that the overall market

design is premised on an excessive seller offer cap and a pay-as-bid clearing mechanism,

neither of which will constrain seller market power in an auction where scarcity is a known

condition.

           The September 29 Order’s primary reasoning for the offer cap amount is that the

$555/MW-day represents the “maximum willingness to pay and process for selecting RBP

resources in the RBP auction.”24 But the order points to no evidence justifying that $555/MW-

day is the maximum willingness to pay in the RBP auction. Instead, FERC states that “PJM

000, available on the FERC e-library website as Accession Document No. 20260821-5317 (“IMM Protest”).

                                                      8
 needs to expeditiously cure the capacity shortage and a high price cap will encourage new

entrants.”25

            FERC also notes that “in establishing the value for the maximum willingness to pay in the

RBP, PJM reasonably relied on the value of the RPM price cap that the Commission accepted in

January and reaffirmed in July” in the RPM quadrennial review of the RPM auction

parameters.”26 But that too fails to explain why the $555/MW-day cap is appropriate for an

auction with known scarcity conditions and no market power mitigation provisions.

             In the RPM quadrennial review proceeding that established $555/MW-day as the upper

bound for procuring capacity in RPM base residual auctions, there are other established measures

in place to mitigate seller market power. As the IMM demonstrates in his Protest, those seller

market power mitigation measures will not exist in the RBP auction. Neither PJM nor FERC

explain why they assume load has a maximum willingness to pay $555/MW-day for capacity to be

procured in the RBP auction where scarcity is highly likely given that the 2028/2029 auction

cleared short by over 6,800 MW. PJM argued in the RBP Application27 that its proposed

“maximum willingness-to-pay cap” will provide “a direct limit on procurement costs even in

the absence of offer mitigation,”28 claiming that “competitive dynamics are expected to

encourage suppliers to submit competitive offers that more closely reflect their willingness to

provide service.”29 But there is no evidence that competitive dynamics are likely to exist in

 the RBP auction. FERC acknowledges that the pay-as-bid nature of the RBP auction is a

“theoretical drawback” to ensuring competitive outcomes, but dismisses this flaw, stating that

this “is acceptable in the context of the proposed $555/MW-day average-price cap and the

Charles River Associates Survey Results indicating strong seller interest in the RBP auction.”30

It is mere speculation that new capacity will show up in the RBP auction in sufficient

quantities to mitigate the known scarcity from the 2028/2029 RPM auction.

           Regardless of the Study results, neither FERC nor PJM explain how the offer cap

will mitigate seller market power when structural market power has long been endemic to

the PJM capacity auctions. The IMM has consistently reported that “[s]tructural market power

is endemic to the capacity market.” 31 In the 2026 State of the Market Report, the IMM states

that “[i]n a good market design and a competitive market structure, market participants are

constrained to behave competitively,” but that “[i]n a market with endemic structural market

power like the PJM Capacity Market, effective market power mitigation rules are required in

order to constrain market participants to behave competitively.”32 Suppliers know they will be

paid their offer price given the pay-as-bid RBP auction design, but there are no rules to

mitigate structural seller market power in that auction.

           The $555/MW-day offer cap FERC accepted in the September 29 Order is more than

$200/MW-day higher than the current collared price cap applied in the 2028/2029 RPM base

residual auction. And while it may make sense that something higher than the cap in the

2028/2029 auction is needed to cure the capacity shortage stemming from that auction, there is no

 justification for why $555/MW-day is the right price point for preventing seller market power in an

auction with known endemic market power, a known shortage to be procured, and a known lack of

market power mitigation measures. The fact that the accepted auction design will pay each seller

whose offer clears the auction its offer bid price for a period of up to 15 years only encourages

rather than discourages offers above competitive levels. While one might argue that a cap above

the clearing price in the last short auction might be needed to encourage new entry, neither PJM

nor FERC explain why $555/MW-day is the right number.

           The obvious goal of a seller offer cap is to mitigate seller market power in the RPM

auctions. FERC has routinely used market seller offer caps in conjunction with an auction

structure that encourages new entrants to bid their marginal cost of new supply into the

auctions.33 FERC found that “a competitive market with a single, market-clearing price creates

incentives for sellers to minimize their costs, because cost-reductions increase a seller’s

profits.”34 FERC further explained that “when many sellers work to minimize their costs,

competition among them keeps prices as low as possible.”35 FERC continued, reasoning that

“[w]hile an efficient seller may, at times, receive revenues that are above its average total costs,

the revenues to an inefficient seller may be below its average total costs and it may be driven out

of business,” and “[t]his market result benefits customers, because over time it results in an

industry with more efficient sellers and lower prices.”36 In Commonwealth Edison Co. FERC

explained that “under this model, the generator has the proper incentive to bid the lowest price

 that covers its marginal cost, knowing that if the market produces a higher price it will receive

the market price.”37

           PJM argued that a single clearing price is inappropriate for the RBP auction design because

that approach would “transfer inframarginal rents to every seller priced below the most expensive

accepted offer.”38 But that concern simply demonstrates the unjustness and unreasonableness of the

excessive offer cap rather than supports a departure from long-held precedent. It is also

inconsistent with FERC’s long-held rulings related to the use of a single clearing price auction

structure for PJM capacity markets.

           FERC does not explain why the goal of RPM, which is to encourage bids reflecting

marginal costs (which addresses market power concerns), is not also needed for the RBP

auction. FERC states only that it recognizes the flaw in pay-as-bid because it does not encourage

marginal cost based bids, but shrugs off that flaw with the argument that the excessive offer cap

and a study indicating strong interest in RBP auction will cure the problem.39 FERC would not

need an excessive offer cap if it was not departing from precedent with the pay-as-bid approach.

It appears that FERC’s hope is that new or more sellers will show up for an auction to be run just

a few months after the 2028/2029 Delivery Year RPM auction which cleared short by more than

6,800 MW. This hope is mere speculation, poses a significant risk of high clearing prices for

consumers, and does not satisfy the judicial requirement for reasoned decision-making.

           Instead of developing a market design consistent with sound economic and FERC policy,

the IMM notes that “PJM’s [RBP] proposals abandon single clearing price logic.”40 As the IMM

 explains, “[b]y proposing a pay as bid auction design with no market power screening, RBP

market sellers have a strong incentive to offer above their costs.”41 There is nothing in that

structure that will prevent sellers from just bidding at the $555/MW-day offer cap regardless of

the sellers’ actual marginal costs. The high offer cap will do nothing to curb seller incentives to

bid above their marginal costs.

           The RBP auction design does not replicate how sellers in competitive markets would bid.

FERC should reconsider its approval of the $555/MW-day offer cap and the pay-as-bid clearing

price auction design because these components of the RBP are unsupported by the evidence and

fail to mitigate seller market power. The September 29 Order fails to explain how the excessive

offer cap in conjunction with a pay-as-bid clearing price design will mitigate seller market power

in the wake of known structural market power that is endemic to the capacity markets, known

capacity shortages in recent auctions, and a lack of market power mitigation measures.

B.         FERC’s approval of the pay-as-bid clearing price mechanism for the RBP auction is
           an unexplained and unreasoned departure from long-held FERC precedent.

              FERC also failed to provide a reasoned explanation for its departure from its long-held

policy of requiring a single clearing price auction design for capacity markets. The September 29

Order attempts to distinguish between the RPM capacity auction design and that approved for

RBP by arguing that pay-as-bid is appropriate when the product to be procured is not uniform.42

But the product to be procured in RBP is just as uniform as it is in the RPM auctions. In the

three-year forward RPM auctions, new capacity participating in the auctions can consist of both

existing and planned generation, as well as demand response resources.43 Similarly, the RBP

     IMM Protest at 12.
42

 auction design approved by FERC allows both existing and planned generating resources and

demand response resources to participate, subject to certain limitations.44 RBP sellers’ capacity

must never have cleared an RPM auction and must have an expected in service date of June 1,

2032.45 While that date is a limitation on sellers that can bid into RBP, the three-year ahead RPM

capacity auctions have a similar start date limitation in that the planned capacity being bid into

the RPM auction must have an in-service date of three years, i.e., by the time the Delivery Year

commences.

           FERC appears to focus on the fact that RBP resources will provide a 15-year

commitment to remain in the market.46 RPM resources have no similar commitment. But that

difference does not mean that the RBP auction design does not seek to procure a uniform

product. The fact remains that bidders into both the RBP and RPM auctions must be available

within the period defined in the respective rules. And while RPM sellers do not have to make

more than a one-year commitment to the market, they nevertheless must offer their capacity into

subsequent auctions unless they satisfy one of four very limited criteria for an exception.47 In

other words, they too have restrictions mandating their participation in the PJM capacity auctions

year-after-year unless they qualify for one of four limited exceptions. That obligation makes

their resources similar to the resources subject to the 15-year participation commitment in the

RBP rules.

           The September 29 Order provides no clear explanation for how FERC decided that RPM

procures a uniform product while RBP does not. FERC describes the uniform product as

 capacity that “may differ based on commercial operation dates and other factors.”48 But there are

limits on commercial operation dates in both the RBP and RPM auctions, as discussed above.

The evidence does not support FERC’s findings. In neither the RBP nor the RPM auction design

is the product to be procured “uniform” as FERC describes that word in the September 29

           The approved RBP pay-as-bid auction design dramatically departs from FERC’s prior

preference for a single auction clearing price structure in order to ensure that market outcomes

are consistent with competitive market conditions. This is inconsistent with Commissioner

LaCerte’s guidance in his concurrence, directing that PJM, in preparing a revised filing, should

“not deviate from the principles of ratepayer protection.”49 Commissioner David Rosner likewise

directed that PJM and its stakeholders must return to market fundamentals so that “[l]oad and

supply should have strong incentives to hedge, manage their risks, and procure the capacity they

rely upon.”50

           FERC never reasonably explained its departure from long-held judicial precedent with

respect to the preference for single clearing price capacity auctions. That unexplained departure

from precedent violates long-held juridical precedent in Williams Gas Processing-Gulf Coast Co.

v. FERC, 475 F.3d 319, 326 (D.C. Cir. 2006) (“Williams Gas Processing”) (citing Brusco Tug &

Barge Co. v. NLRB, 247 F.3d 273, 278 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (“[I]t is ‘axiomatic that [agency action]

must either be consistent with prior [action] or offer a reasoned basis for its departure from

precedent’”). This failure to explain its departure requires rehearing or reconsideration by FERC

of this ruling.
